clue.text: See 11
Barn, I guess, is deployed for farmers' market

indicators.note: troops deployed are spread out and rearranged, so the preceding letters are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A farmer sizes up a barn being put to use for a weekly market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is deployed' signals the anagram of BARN I GUESS IS; the second 'is' is fodder, the first part of the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Large-scale commercial agriculture is the trade that sells to, and buys from, farmers: their market in a broad sense.

clue.text: Beat or scrap

parts.note: a scrap is a small bit

explanation.surface: Someone is told to strike out or throw away their plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like a verb of hitting; it is the noun, a regular round or circuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A policeman's beat is the regular circuit he patrols, a sense also carried by an orbit or sphere of activity.

clue.text: Knots increasing as one ties the knot

parts.note: hitches are kinds of knot
prices going up are increasing

explanation.surface: A sailor's knots multiply as he gets married.
explanation.definitionFit: To get hitched, or hitch up, is informal for marrying, the same idiom as tying the knot.

clue.text: Dead right I see to invade retrospective performance

indicators.note: looking back, so the whole assembled string is read from end to start
one group invading another goes inside it, so I and C go into the word for dead

parts.note: the late someone is dead
the letter C is said like see

explanation.surface: A gloomy retrospective show is gatecrashed by someone saying they see the point.
explanation.walkthrough: IC goes inside LATE to give LATICE; add R for LATICER, and 'retrospective' reads that backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a performance, typically of music or poetry by one or a few players.

clue.text: Have too many hands on the isle?

parts.note: on top of something is over it
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, is commonly just Man

explanation.surface: A question whether an island workforce is overstaffed.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'on the isle' as 'over Man', the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: To overman a ship or factory is to give it more workers, hands, than it needs.

clue.text: Sail free from Alistair Campbell's pursuit? One's beaten!

indicators.note: the sail is to be freed of a run of its letters, so they are taken out

parts.note: a spinnaker is a large racing sail
Alastair Campbell, Tony Blair's press chief, was the archetypal spin doctor, so spin was his trade

explanation.surface: Escaping a pursuit by Blair's spin doctor, someone ends up thrashed.
explanation.walkthrough: Alastair Campbell was Downing Street's director of communications, famous for spin; SPINNAKER without SPIN leaves the kettledrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A naker is a medieval kettledrum, an instrument one beats.

clue.text: They make good pictures

parts.note: read not as good photographers but as people who make good, that is repair, damaged paintings

explanation.definitionFit: Art restorers repair and clean damaged paintings, making them good again.

clue.text: R1-O2, BT's version of R2-D2?

indicators.note: a version is another form of something, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: read as one R and two Os
the letters B and T as printed

explanation.surface: A telecom company's own model of the Star Wars droid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'R1-O2' looks like a droid name but counts letters: R once, O twice.
explanation.definitionFit: R2-D2 is the robot from the Star Wars films, given here as an example with a question mark.

clue.text: As Pooter, Cratchit and Heep relish KC's blunder

indicators.note: a blunder messes things up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Three fictional clerks enjoy a barrister's mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: Pooter (Diary of a Nobody), Bob Cratchit (A Christmas Carol) and Uriah Heep (David Copperfield) are all clerks; KC is King's Counsel, a senior barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: All three are famous fictional office clerks, so they are characteristically clerk-like.

clue.text: Block booking cancelled? So stay cool!

definitions.meaning: an execution on the block called off, so the prisoner's head stays on

explanation.surface: A group reservation falls through, and the organiser is urged not to panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block booking' looks like a group reservation; it is an appointment with the executioner's block.
explanation.definitionFit: Not losing one's head is the idiom for staying calm in a crisis.

clue.text: The words 23 needed when accused in huntin' his totty at random …

definitions.text: The words 23 needed when accused in huntin' his totty at random …

parts.words: The words 23 needed when accused in huntin' his totty at random
parts.note: Barabas, in Marlowe's The Jew of Malta, accused of fornication, shrugs it off with a famous line about time, place and the woman's death

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into 12-across, naming the play's author.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Barabas's reply to the charge of fornication in The Jew of Malta, Act IV, a much-quoted dismissal.

clue.text: … by moral degeneracy we observed in a Deptford stabbing victim

indicators.note: degeneracy is a falling into corrupt disorder, so the letters are disarranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the tale: moral decline seen in a man knifed in Deptford.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Marlowe was stabbed to death in a house in Deptford, south-east London, in 1593; 'observed in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright Christopher Marlowe died of a knife wound in Deptford in 1593.

clue.text: See 11
Perform poem in that dreadful silence!

parts.note: to do is to perform

indicators.note: the poem goes inside the rearranged letters
dreadful suggests something mangled, so the letters of that are jumbled

parts.note: an ode is a poem

explanation.surface: Reciting verse in that awful hush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silence!' looks like a command for quiet, but it is the verb in its sense of killing; 'dreadful' scrambles that, and 'in' signals the insertion of the poem.
explanation.definitionFit: To silence someone permanently is to kill them, which is what doing to death means.

clue.text: Hibernation protracted huntsman's return

parts.note: drawn out, so long

indicators.note: a return goes back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: John Peel was the Cumbrian huntsman of the song D'ye ken John Peel

explanation.surface: A huntsman comes home after a long winter's rest.
explanation.walkthrough: John Peel was a famous Lake District fox hunter, celebrated in a folk song.
explanation.definitionFit: Hibernating animals spend the winter in a prolonged torpor, a lengthy sleep.

clue.text: Scavengers to slip through waste's disposal

indicators.note: disposal also means arrangement, so the letters are set out anew

parts.note: to err is to slip up

explanation.surface: Rubbish slips down a waste disposal unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposal' is the anagram signal on ERR and WASTES; 'through' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Rats living in drains feed on refuse, a classic scavenger.

clue.text: New poet spilling half preprandial drink with his tablet

indicators.note: spilling scatters things, so the letters are rearranged
the first half of the drink's name is kept

parts.note: an aperitif is drunk before a meal

explanation.surface: A new poet knocks over half his aperitif onto his writing tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' keeps APER from APERITIF; 'spilling' jumbles POET into OTEP.
explanation.definitionFit: A tablet can be a pad of writing paper, the stationery for letters.

clue.text: Training note: "Preserve emergency rations!"

parts.note: PE is physical education, training at school
mi is a note of the sol-fa scale
to can food is to preserve it

explanation.surface: A drill instruction to keep back the survival rations.
explanation.definitionFit: Pemmican, also spelt pemican, is dried meat pounded with fat, carried as concentrated travel food.

clue.text: Refuse to criticise

explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish is household refuse, and to rubbish something is to criticise it scornfully.

clue.text: See 11
Rod Stewart's first idea jolly!

indicators.note: only the opening letter of Stewart's is used

parts.note: taken as written
a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, RM

explanation.surface: An excited remark about the singer Rod Stewart's first notion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' looks like the singer's first name, but it is the definition: US slang for a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A rod is gangster slang for a handgun, a weapon worn at the side.

clue.text: Unknowingly, Longfellow lost this quarrel

definitions.meaning: in Longfellow's poem The ... and the Song the speaker shoots one into the air and knows not where it falls
a bolt shot from a crossbow

explanation.surface: A poet unwittingly lost an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarrel is the square-headed bolt fired from a crossbow, a kind of shaft.

clue.text: Born Arab, like 12's Jew from Valletta?

parts.note: taken as written
as means like

explanation.surface: Asks whether Marlowe's Maltese Jew was born an Arab.
explanation.walkthrough: Barabas is the title character of Marlowe's The Jew of Malta; Valletta is Malta's capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Barabas is the Jew of Malta in Marlowe's play, so he is the playwright's Maltese Jew.

clue.text: Hector has no right to the insignia

definitions.note: plural in form, but used for a single emblem here

indicators.note: the word lacks the letter, so it is dropped

parts.note: to hector is to badger or bully

explanation.surface: Hector, the Trojan hero, has no claim to the emblems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hector' looks like a name; it is the verb to hector.
explanation.definitionFit: An insignia is a distinguishing emblem of rank or membership, which is what a badge shows.

clue.text: Free music! Which publishers cut-price Charles Ives overtures?

parts.note: Which? magazine is published by the Consumers' Association, CA

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its last letter
openings, so the first letters of the two names

explanation.surface: A query about which firm sells cheap editions of Charles Ives, offering music for free.
explanation.walkthrough: Which? is a British consumer magazine from the Consumers' Association; 'cut' trims PRICE to PRIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Capriccios are lively pieces in free form, so the plural names free-form music.
